subject: FSCI
description: Introduction to the theory and practice of science communication and outreach. Emphasis is placed on inclusive practices. Audience needs and existing critiques of current outreach and communication practice.
restrictions: Open to graduate students and undergraduates in Year 2or higher. Students in Year 0 or Year 1 may request instructor approval to register.

title: Introduction to Automation and Control
subject: GEAC
description: Fundamental concepts to analyze the behavior of dynamic systems and determination of control laws, Systems modelling, Transfer functions, Open and closed- loop system analysis, PID Control, State feedback and observers.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Robotics Bootcamp
subject: GEAC
description: Mini projects centered around concrete design of command and embedded systems of the Arduino type.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEAC 211, Intro to Automation & Control.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Cell Biology
subject: GEBI
description: Molecular characteristics and physicochemical principles, small organic molecules, Metabolic transformations.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Basic secondary level knowledge of biology.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Genetics
subject: GEBI
description: Structures of genes and genomes, DNA structure, gene structure, Structures of prokaryotic & eukaryotic genomes.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Cell Biology and Genetics
subject: GEBI
description: Molecular characteristics and physicochemical principles, small organic molecules, Metabolic transformations. Structures of genes and genomes, DNA structure, gene structure, Structures of prokaryotic eukaryotic genomes.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Introduction to Bioengineering
subject: GEBI
description: Introduction & basic concepts, design in bioengineering & biomaterials, cell mechanics, properties of biological matter.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Ecosystems and Biodiversity
subject: GEBI
description: Key concepts revolving around biodiversity, 4 types of major ecosystems, evolution of ecological thinking.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: General Chemistry: Atomistics and Bonding
subject: GECH
description: Origins of elementary particles, global concept between matter and energy, covalent bonding.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Proficiency at a high school level in chemistry, physics, and mathematics is required.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Chemistry of Solutions
subject: GECH
description: Chemical kinetics, Laws of chemical equilibrium, Chemical reactions in the solution, acid-base titration.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Chemistry 1: General Chemistry and Thermochemistry
subject: GECH
description: Origins of elementary particles, global concept between matter and energy, covalent bonding. Transformation models, description parameters in a chemical physics system, standard quantities standard reaction quantities, thermal effects of a reaction.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Oxidation, Reduction and Electrochemistry
subject: GECH
description: Reduction-oxidation equilibrium, redox couple, reduction- oxidation reaction, reversible battery electrode.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GECH 111, General Chemistry. GECH 112, Chemistry of Solutions.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Chem 2: Solutions, Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochem
subject: GECH
description: Chemical kinetics, Laws of chemical equilibrium, Chemical reactions in the solution, acid-base titration. Reduction-oxidation equilibrium, redox couple, reduction-oxidation reaction, reversible battery electrode.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Thermochemistry
subject: GECH
description: Transformation models, description parameters in a chemical physics system, standard quantities & standard reaction quantities, thermal effects of a reaction.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GECH 111, General Chemistry. GECH 112, Chemistry of Solutions. GEPH 121, Thermodynamics.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Introduction to Programming
subject: GECS
description: Fundamentals of databases: database design & SQL, programming in Python, variables, collections, loops, functions.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Coding Weeks
subject: GECS
description: Intensive software development, digital management tools & programing environments, web-oriented programing.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Computer Science 1: Algorithms and Intro to Programming
subject: GECS
description: Fundamentals of databases: database design & SQL, programming in Python, variables, collections, loops, functions. Abstract algorithmics, Discrete mathematical tools, sorting methods, data structures, stacks, queues, heaps. Computer architecture, Processes memory management, Networks: OSI model, introduction to information security.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Algorithms
subject: GECS
description: Abstract algorithmics, Discrete mathematical tools, sorting methods, data structures, stacks, queues, heaps.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 121, Analysis 3. GECS 111, Introduction to Programming
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Fundamentals of programming: Information Systems
subject: GECS
description: Computer architecture, Processes & memory management, Networks: OSI model, introduction to information security.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GECS 111, Introduction to Programming. GECS 112, Coding Week.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Comp Sci 2: Advanced Programming and Machine Learning
subject: GECS
description: Computer architecture, Processes memory management, Networks: OSI model, introduction to information security. Introduce methods algorithms used in machine learning present some fundamentals of artificial intelligence.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Advanced Programming
subject: GECS
description: Object-oriented programming paradigm (OOP) by means of the JAVA programming language, “procedural” elements.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: None (though previous experience with computer programming might help).
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Advanced Programming
subject: GECS
description: Object-oriented programming paradigm (OOP) by means of the JAVA programming language, “procedural” elements.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: None (though previous experience with computer programming might help).
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Machine Learning
subject: GECS
description: Introduce methods & algorithms used in machine learning & present some fundamentals of artificial intelligence.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Organizational Behavior Week
subject: GEEC
description: Overview of corporate structures, org of corporate entities, org of intl NGOs & Supranational Structures.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEHS 121, Topics in International Sustainable Development 1.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Business Strategy and Corporate Finance
subject: GEEC
description: Economic cycles, instability and growth, sustainability, key macroeconomic indicators & their relationships.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEHS 221, Structure of Corporations. GEEC 221, Organizational Behaviour Week.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Business Games Week
subject: GEEC
description: Exploration of the different functions of a company through a role-playing game in which each student plays the rôle of a company executive adapting to market conditions.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEHS 211, Perspectives of Modern Geopolitics 1.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Elective
subject: GEEE
description: The list of electives will be defined at a later date, based on the needs in terms of prerequisites in order to ensure the comfortable operability of stream choices at McGill.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Philosophy, Ethics and Critical Thinking 1&2
subject: GEHS
description: Cornerstone of an approach based on rich, high quality “critical thinking”, legitimate scientific knowledge.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Sustainable Development, Environmental Economics and Policy
subject: GEHS
description: Introduction to Sustainable Development & Energy & Environmental Economics, global warming.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: This course is linked to the work in project GEPR 121.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Principles of Microeconomics and Industrial Organization
subject: GEHS
description: Ind trade & geo-economics, globalization & intl trade, Economies of Scale & Intl Location of Production.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Introduction to Geopolitics & Geoeconomics
subject: GEHS
description: Microeconomics & Ind Org, Consumer theory, Partial equilibrium, applications in antitrust & competition policy.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Internship - Social Impact
subject: GEIN
description: Involvement in an international organization for at least 6- weeks, the internship requires a written report.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Professional Discovery Internship (PDI)
subject: GEIN
description: Immersion in a business with a strong international focus, writing of a report & presentation to the cohort.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Analysis 1
subject: GEMA
description: Ordinary differential equations (ODE), modern mathematical formalism, mathematical theory, finite probabilities, Simulation random variables using Python, regular functions (differentiable, convex, Lipschitz, Taylorexpansion).
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Analysis 2
subject: GEMA
description: Linear transformations, linear systems, quadrics, Markov processes, correlation structures.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 111, Analysis 1. GEPH 111, Mechanics. GEPH 112, Electric Circuits.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Mathematics 1: Real Analysis and Linear Algebra
subject: GEMA
description: Ordinary differential equations (ODE), modern mathematical formalism, mathematical theory, finite probabilities, Simulation random variables using Python, regular functions (differentiable, convex, Lipschitz, Taylor expansion). Linear transformations, linear systems, quadrics, Markov processes, correlation structures.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Analysis 3
subject: GEMA
description: Norm topology, multi-dimensional integration, differential calculus, Jacobian matrix, chain rule.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Probability
subject: GEMA
description: Discrete probability, count elements in a set, model a random experiment, important notions in probability.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Mathematics 2 : Multivariable Real Analysis and Probability
subject: GEMA
description: Norm topology, multi-dimensional integration, differential calculus, Jacobian matrix, chain rule. Discrete probability, count elements in a set, model a random experiment, important notions in probability.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Linear Algebra
subject: GEMA
description: Linear algebra, complements, numerical linear algebra, determinant – complements, polynomials, matrix reduction.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Topology and Functional Analysis
subject: GEMA
description: Notion of approximation, Normed topology, complements, Integral and Lp spaces, Hilbert spaces, Fouriertransform.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 121, Analysis 3. GEMA 122, Probability. GEMA 211, Linear Algebra.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Linear Algebra and functional analysis
subject: GEMA
description: Linear algebra, complements, numerical linear algebra, determinant – complements, polynomials, matrix reduction. Notion of approximation, Normed topology, complements, Integral and Lp spaces, Hilbert spaces, Fourier transform.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Numerical Analysis
subject: GEMA
description: Classes of problems in applied mathematics, solving a linear system, computing the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, minimizing a function.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 211, Linear Algebra. GEMA 112, Analysis 2. GEMA 121, Analysis 3.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Continuous Probability & Intro to Statistical Modelling
subject: GEMA
description: Knowledge in probability, Gaussian distribution, statistical modeling, statistical inference, parametric estimation.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 122, Probability. GEMA 212, Topology and Functional Analysis.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Mathematics 4 :  Integration, Probability and Statistics
subject: GEMA
description: Classes of problems in applied mathematics, solving a linear system, computing the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, minimizing a function. Knowledge in probability, Gaussian distribution, statistical modeling, statistical inference, parametric estimation.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Modern Languages 1
subject: GEML
description: French as a foreign language for non-francophone students, professional communication skills: Rhetoric & Debate.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Modern Languages 2
subject: GEML
description: French as a foreign language for non-francophone students; professional communication skills, rhetoric & debate.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Modern Languages 3
subject: GEML
description: French as a foreign language: for non-francophone students; professional communication skills: Professional scientific writing.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Modern Languages 4
subject: GEML
description: French language, for non-francophone students; professional communication & scientific writing skills.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering students.

title: Introduction to Modelling
subject: GEMO
description: Multi-disciplinary course, modeling challenge by team, epidemiology, climate science and aeronautics.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEMA 111. GEMA 112. GEPH 111. GEPH 112. GECH 111. GECH 112. GEBI 111. GECS 111. GECS 112.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Data and Modelling Week
subject: GEMO
description: Projects in mini-groups co-supervised by a professional engineer on an interdisciplinary-type subject.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: The whole assignment brings together the cross-section of scientific knowledge covered in earlier courses.
restrictions: Open only to Global Engineering Students.

title: Geographical Perspectives: World Environmental Problems
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to geography as the study of nature and human beings in a spatial context. An integrated approach to environmental systems and the human organization of them from the viewpoint of spatial relationships and processes. Special attention to environmental problems as a constraint upon Third World development.

title: Introductory Geo-Information Science
subject: GEOG
description: An introduction to Geographic Information Systems. The systematic management of spatial data. The use and construction of maps. The use of microcomputers and software for mapping and statistical work. Air photo and topographic map analyses.

title: Statistics and Spatial Analysis
subject: GEOG
description: Exploratory data analysis, univariate descriptive and inferential statistics, non-parametric statistics, correlation and simple regression. Problems associated with analysing spatial data such as the 'modifiable areal unit problem' and spatial autocorrelation. Statistics measuring spatial pattern in point, line and polygon data.

title: Environmental Systems
subject: GEOG
description: An introduction to system-level interactions among climate, hydrology, soils and vegetation at the scale of drainage basins, including the study of the global geographical variability in these land-surface systems. The knowledge acquired is used to study the impact on the environment of various human activities such as deforestation and urbanisation.
restrictions: Because of quantitative science content of course, not recommended for B.A. and B.Ed. students in their U0 year.

title: Global Change: Past, Present and Future
subject: GEOG
description: An examination of global change, from the Quaternary Period to the present day involving changes in the physical geography of specific areas. Issues such as climatic change and land degradation will be discussed, with speculations on future environments.

title: Global Places and Peoples
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to key themes in human geography. Maps and the making, interpretation and contestation of landscapes, 'place', and territory. Investigation of globalization and the spatial organization of human geo-politics, and urban and rural environments.

title: Geography of the World Economy
subject: GEOG
description: The course introduces the geography of the world economic system. It describes the spatial distribution of economic activities and examines the factors which influence their changing location. Case studies from both "developed" and "developing" countries will test the different geographical theories presented in lectures.

title: Cities in the Modern World
subject: GEOG
description: An introduction to urban geography. Uses a spatial/geographic perspective to understand cities and their social and cultural processes. Addresses two major areas. The development and social dynamics in North American and European cities. The urban transformations in Asian, African, and Latin American societies that were recently predominantly rural and agrarian.

title: Environment and Health
subject: GEOG
description:
Key chemical, physical, and social stressors in the environment, and how these affect the health of people and ecosystems. Hazards in air, water, food, and work environments. Historic, current, and future need for environmental health
science, from scientific, personal, and practical perspectives.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking NRSC 221.

title: Earth's Changing Surface
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to the study of landforms as products of geomorphic and geologic systems acting at and near the Earth's surface. The process geomorphology approach will be used to demonstrate how landforms of different geomorphic settings represent a dynamic balance between forces acting in the environment and the physical properties of materials present.

title: Local Geographical Excursion
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to landscape interpretation and geographical site analysis in physical and human geography. A three-day fall excursion with preparatory and concluding seminars.
restrictions: Open to first-year Geography Major and Honours students only.

title: Independent Short  Project in Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Under the guidance of an instructor with the relevant expertise, the student explores a research topic in Geography and develops a written report.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 201 and one of: GEOG 203, GEOG 210, GEOG 216, GEOG 217, GEOG 272
restrictions: Restricted to students enrolled in the Geography Core Science Component, Major, Major Concentration and Honours programs. Instructor (supervisor) approval required.

title: Human Ecology in Geography
subject: GEOG
description: The course will examine research approaches in human ecology since its inception early in this century. Emphasis will be placed on the theoretical shifts that have led to its emergence as an important social science perspective. The course will also involve case studies to evaluate the methodological utility of the approach.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 203 or ANTH 202 or BIOL 111

title: Geography of Nunavut
subject: GEOG
description: An introduction to the physical and cultural geography of Canada's newest territory. The course will emphasize the bio-physical heterogeneity of the natural environment and the cultural and political ecology of the human population.

title: Environmental Management 1
subject: GEOG
description: An ecological analysis of the physical and biotic components of natural resource systems. Emphasis on scientific, technological and institutional aspects of environmental management. Study of the use of biological resources and of the impact of individual processes.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Any 200-level course in Geography or MSE or BIOL 308 or permission of instructor.

title: Health Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Discussion of the research questions and methods of health geography. Particular emphasis on health inequalities at multiple geographic scales and the theoretical links between characteristics of places and the health of people.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: One of the following: ENVR 201; GEOG 201, GEOG 203, GEOG 210, GEOG 216, GEOG 217; or permission of the instructor.

title: Soils and Environment
subject: GEOG
description: Discussion of the major properties of soils; soil formation, classification and mapping; land capability assessment; the role and response of soils in natural and disturbed environments (e.g. global change, ecosystem disturbance).
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 203 or introductory course in biology or geology

title: Remote Sensing for Earth Observation
subject: GEOG
description: A conceptual view of remote sensing and the underlying physical principles. Covers ground-based, aerial, satellite systems, and the electromagnetic spectrum, from visible to microwave. Emphasis on application of remotely sensed data in geography including land cover change and ecological processes.
corequisitesText: Corequisite: GEOG 201 or permission of instructor

title: Development and Livelihoods
subject: GEOG
description: Geographical dimensions of rural/urban livelihoods in the face of socioeconomic and environmental change in developing regions. Emphasis on household natural resource use, survival strategies and vulnerability, decision-making, formal and informal institutions, migration, and development experience in contrasting global environments.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 210 or GEOG 216 or ENVR 201 or INTD 200

title: Economic Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Different theories and approaches to understanding the spatial organization of economic activities. Regional case studies drawn from North America, Europe and Asia used to reinforce concepts. Emphasis also on city-regions and their interaction with the global economy.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 216 or permission of instructor

title: Geospatial Analysis
subject: GEOG
description: Overview of both the theoretical and applied aspects of geographic information science and systems. Topics will include spatial analysis techniques, geographic models as abstractions of the real world, spatial data manipulation and management, and conceptual issues related to geographic data and technology. Introduction to  a number of leading commercial software including ESRI’s ArcGIS Pro.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken GEOG 306 or GEOG 307.

title: Urban Transportation Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Discusses the history and development of urban transportation systems, as well as problems and potential solutions from a geographic perspective. Specific topics include analysis of the social, economic, and environmental impacts; interaction of land use and transportation systems; the analysis of urban travel behaviour; and the implications of various policy alternatives.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 217 or permission of instructor

title: Political Geography
subject: GEOG
description: The study of the spatial dimensions of political activities and developments at the regional, national and global levels in historical and contemporary perspective. Presentation of case studies relating to the theoretical framework of political geography.

title: Climatic Environments
subject: GEOG
description: The earth-atmosphere system, radiation and energy balances. Surface-atmosphere exchange of energy, mass and momentum and related atmospheric processes on a local and regional scale. Introduction to measurement theory and practice in micrometeorology.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 203 or ATOC 210 or permission of instructor

title: Environmental Hydrology
subject: GEOG
description: Quantitative, experimental study of the principles governing the movement of water at or near the Earth's surface and how the research relates to the chemistry and biology of ecosystems.

title: New Master-Planned Cities
subject: GEOG
description: This course examines the origins, designs, motivations and cultural politics of planned cities, focusing primarily on those currently under construction in Africa, the Middle East and Asia. A variety of themes will be explored including design responses to urban pollution and over-crowding, 'new' cities from earlier decades, totalitarianism and the city, utopianism, 'green' cities, and 'creative' cities. The course examines the various motivations underlying the design and construction of planned cities and how they are shaped by power, religion, and political ideologies. There will be a focus on evolving concepts used in city design as well as the continuities and cultural revivalism expressed through urban design and architecture. Students interested in urban and cultural geography, cities, architecture and planning in different cultural contexts will enjoy this course.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 217, or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Open to U2 and above students.

title: Urban Social Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Social space and social time. The reflection of social structure in the spatial organization of the city. Historical perspective on changing personal mobility, life cycle, family structure and work organization. The appropriation and alienation of urban spaces.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 216 or GEOG 217 or permission of instructor

title: Introduction to Programming for Spatial Sciences
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to conceptual and practical aspects of programming for the spatial sciences, focusing on programming concepts and techniques irrespective of the specific programming language, framework, or software. Topics include spatial data structures, flow control, classes and objects, and basics of geospatial data modeling and analysis.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking COMP 202, COMP 204, or COMP 208. May be taken before COMP 206 orCOMP 250, but not concurrently with or after either course. Not open to students who have taken GEOG 407 in Fall 2019 or 2020.

title: Sustainability in the Caribbean
subject: GEOG
description:
The local environmental, social, historical, political and economic context of Barbados and the Caribbean. The small island developing States (SIDS), and why those nations are more vulnerable to global environmental challenges. The 17
Sustainability Development Goals of the United Nations, with a focus on the leadership role played by Barbados for the entire Caribbean region.
corequisitesText: Corequisites: ATOC 341, BIOL 343, FSCI 444 or permission of the Program Director.
restrictions: Open to U2 and U3 students from all faculties who are registered in the Barbados Field Study Semester, with minimum CGPA of 3.0.

title: Ecological Biogeography
subject: GEOG
description: The study of the patterns of distribution of organisms in space and time with emphasis on plant communities. Ecological, geographical, historical and anthropological factors affecting these distribution patterns will be discussed. Particular consideration is given to methods for description and classification of plant communities.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 203 or ENVR 200 or ENVR 202

title: Quantitative Methods
subject: GEOG
description: Multiple regression and correlation, logit models, discrete choice models, gravity models, facility location algorithms, survey design, population projection.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 202 or equivalent or permission of instructor

title: Analyzing Sustainability
subject: GEOG
description: Examines challenges to sustainability through a series of case studies to illustrate the analytical approaches used to understand the linkages between scientific-technological, socio-economic, political-institutional, ethical, and human behavioural aspect of systems. Includes cases that are thematic and place-based, national and international, spanning from the local to global scales.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: ENVR 201 or equivalent; and GEOG 203 or ENVR 200 or ESYS 200 or equivalent; or permission of instructor

title: Running Water Environments
subject: GEOG
description: The course focuses on the physical habitat conditions found in streams, rivers, estuaries and deltas. Based on the laws governing flow of water and sediment transport, it emphasizes differences among these environments, in terms of channel form, flow patterns, substrate composition and mode of evolution. Flooding, damming, channelisation, forestry impacts.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 203 and GEOG 272, or ENVR 200 and ENVR 202

title: Arctic Geomorphology
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to the principles of periglacial and permafrost science and its field context in the Canadian North. Objectives focus on the geomorphic significance of freezing and frozen ground and training in field methods of permafrost mapping, measurement and interpretation.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 203, GEOG 205, GEOG 272, GEOG 372, ENVR 200, ENVR 202, EPSC 203, EPSC 210, EPSC 212, EPSC 220, EPSC 233, ATOC 214, ATOC 215, ATOC 219, SOIL 300.
corequisitesText: Corequisite(s): ATOC 373, EPSC 373, [ATOC 473 or EPSC 473 or GEOG 473]

title: Geographic Thought and Practice
subject: GEOG
description: Critical perspectives of the history and practice of the discipline, considering different paradigms and theoretical approaches that have been influential in its development. Possible methods, ethical debates, and other processes involved in conducting geographical research.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Departmental advisor permission is required.
restrictions: Open to U2 B.A. and B.Sc. Honours and Joint Honours in Geography, and B.A. Honours in Urban Studies students.

title: Principles of Geospatial Web
subject: GEOG
description: Theory and practice of geospatial web, including examining spatial data accuracy and uncertainty of user generated content; Understanding motivations of contributors of volunteered geographic information for purposes like citizen science and crisis mapping; Critically evaluating political, societal, economic and legal issues in online mapping applications; Developing geospatial applications and identifying basic problem solving requirements for geospatial apps. For proposed  solutions, evaluating and justifying various existing and emergent geospatial technologies and enabling software stacks; Exploring underlying methods of digital earth architectures; Understanding implications to geospatial analysis and visualization of real time streaming data and mobile sensors
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 201; GEOG 333 or COMP 202; and GEOG 314; or permission of the instructor.

title: Undergraduate Research Project
subject: GEOG
description: Independent research project with a final written report.
restrictions: This course cannot be taken under the S/U option. Departmental permission required. Students cannot be supervised by the same instructor for two 396 Science courses. Open to students in programs offered by the Faculty of Science only.

title: Field Studies in Human Geography
subject: GEOG
description:
Introduction to human geography, field methods, observational techniques, and data collection, processing and analysis. Applying a range of field techniques of the practical and ethical challenges in gathering data used in social science research. How to apply methods and techniques related to human geography, such as social survey design, interviewing (focus groups, structured interviews, oral histories), participant
observation, community profiling, land use/cover mapping and assessment, social network analysis, ecosystem service valuation, and impact valuation.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Any introductory human geography course; or by permission of the instructor

title: Socio-Environmental Systems: Theory and Simulation
subject: GEOG
description: Conceptual and simulation models of key case studies for developing system thinking, including system stability, threshold dynamics in regime shifts, resilience, and adaptive environmental management.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: ENVR 201, GEOG 360, and two of the following courses: ENVR 200, ENVR 202, ENVR 203 and GEOG 203.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken GEOG 501, or GEOG 407 when topic was "Socio-Environmental Systems."

title: Global Health and Environmental Change
subject: GEOG
description: Major themes and contemporary case studies in global health and environmental change. Focus on understanding global trends in emerging infectious disease from social, biophysical, and geographical perspectives, and critically assessing the health implications of environmental change in different international contexts.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 205 or GEOG 221 or GEOG 321 or GEOG 303 or permission from the instructor
restrictions: Course not open to students who were registered for GEOG 303 in Winter 2008.

title: Environmental Management 2
subject: GEOG
description: Practical application of environmental planning, analysis and management techniques with reference to the needs and problems of developing areas. Special challenges posed by cultural differences and traditional resource systems are discussed. This course involves practical field work in a developing area (Kenya or Panama).
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 302 or permission of instructor

title: Issues in Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Treatment of contemporary issues in geographical research focusing on human-environmental relations and interactions. Instructor(s) and topics will be announced each term the course is given.

title: Geography of Development
subject: GEOG
description: Examines the geographical dimensions of development policy, specifically the relationships between the process of development and human-induced environmental change. Focuses on environmental sustainability, struggles over resource control, population and poverty, and levels of governance (the role of the state, non-governmental organizations, and local communities).
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 210 or GEOG 216 or permission of instructor

title: Geographies of Developing Asia
subject: GEOG
description: Current development questions that are of concern to the Asian region. Emphasis on critically studying the major processes of social, economic and environmental change through regional case studies in rural, peri-urban and urban contexts. Covers important debates and considerations that lie at the heart of development geography.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 210 or GEOG 216 or ENVR 201 or INTD 200 or GEOG 310 or permission of instructor

title: Advanced Geospatial Analysis
subject: GEOG
description:
Advanced techniques in geospatial analysis. Geospatial methods and using geospatial information systems. Topics: geodatabases, interpolation techniques, spatial
classification methods, data mining and machine learning, including working with a number of leading commercial software including ESRI’s ArcGIS Desktop/Pro.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 314; and GEOG 333 or COMP 202; or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken GEOG 306 or GEOG 307.

title: Africa South of the Sahara
subject: GEOG
description: A synthetic overview of physical and cultural geography examining particularly the relation of African peoples to their landscapes, the causes and consequences of environmental changes, and the idea of sustainable development as it applies to African landscapes, resource systems and economies.

title: Urban Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Classic and contemporary perspectives in urban geography. Range of topics including effects of capitalism, gender, suburbanism, segregation and inequality, property, urban landscapes, and urban space. Emphasizes theoretical issues but includes empirical and/or case studies.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 217, and one of the following: GEOG 315, GEOG 316, GEOG 325, GEOG 331, or GEOG 525; or permission of the instructor.

title: Geographies of Race
subject: GEOG
description:
Exploration of some ways race and racism manifest spatially, including how race and racism shape vast built environments in addition to intimate experiences of
space. Historical, political, and cultural insight for the ongoing racial politics of place.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 216 or GEOG 217, or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken GEOG 407 in Fall 2022.

title: Memory, Place, and Power
subject: GEOG
description:
This interdisciplinary class explores the relationships among memory, place, and political power. The course begins with an introduction to key classical, Enlightenment, and contemporary texts on memory and place-making. It then uses
this foundation to examine the symbolic transformation of public space, in particular the construction, alteration, and destruction of monuments, memorials, and museums in postcommunist states and in North America. This approach emphasizes the social quality of memory, exploring the ways in which political
interests, economic resources, and social practices can shape something as ostensibly personal and individual as memory.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): One of the following: GEOG 316, GEOG 325, or GEOG 331; or one 200- or 300-level course in Comparative Politics required; or permission of instructor.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking POLI 420, or who have taken POLI 432 when topic was "Memory, Place, and Power”.

title: Dilemmas of Development
subject: GEOG
description: Africa seems beset by development problems. Some of these appear to have no clear answer. Such dilemmas present significant barriers to moving forward with durable, effective development in Africa. This course will examine two primary and frequently interlocked dilemmas in East Africa with wide ranging impact - food security, and conflict.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 310 or GEOG 408 or GEOG 410, or equivalent
restrictions: Open to students in the African Field Study Semester (AFSS) only

title: Southeast Asia Urban Field Studies
subject: GEOG
description: This course allows students to experience some of the urban changes taking place in Southeast Asian cities, a dynamic region, while providing the opportunity to connect recent scholarship with field observations. We will explore various current themes in urban studies and urban geography including globalization, the transnational circulation of urban policies, interpretations of culture and heritage / new built heritage, gentrification, migrant labour, public housing, creative clusters, and new cities as national economic strategies.
restrictions: Preference will be given to Urban Studies Majors and Minors

title: Earth System Geographic Information Science
subject: GEOG
description: Foundational concepts, methods and techniques in Geographic Information Science (GIS) to manage, process, interpret, understand, and analyze digital geospatial land surface data for a variety of Earth system applications, with a special focus on global hydrology. Emphasis will be placed on recognizing issues of resolution, scale, data accuracy and uncertainties.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite (s): GEOG 201; and one of the following: GEOG 308, GEOG 314; or permission of the instructor
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking ENVB 529 or BREE 529

title: Sand in the Anthropocene
subject: GEOG
description: A critical examination of the increasing global consumption of sand resources and the human-causedchanges and impact on sediment dynamics, landscape evolution, ecological processes in freshwater ecosystemand conservation biology.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 272 or BIOL 206 or EPSC 355 or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking BIOL 438. Not open to students who have taken GEOG 407 in winter 2025 under the topic: "Sand in the Anthropocene".

title: Research in Society and Development in Africa
subject: GEOG
description: Three intersecting components: 1) core development themes including culture change, environmental conservation, water, health, development (urban and rural), governance and conflict resolution, 2) research techniques for topics related to core themes, including ethics, risk, field methods and data analysis, 3) field documentation, scientific recording and communication.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Open to U2 or later students in the AFSS.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken, or are taking ANTH 451.

title: Research in Sustainability
subject: GEOG
description: Through engaging in real-world sustainability challenges through hands-on research, learn to critically analyze problems that arise at the interface of multiple disciplines including the scientific-technological, socio-economic, political-institutional, ethical, and human behavioural. Develop an understanding of the leverages and road blocks in achieving a sustainability transition.

title: Wetlands
subject: GEOG
description: An examination of the structure, function and utility of wetlands. Topics include the fluxes of energy and water, wetland biogeochemistry, plant ecology in freshwater and coastal wetlands and wetlands use, conservation and restoration. Field trip(s) are envisaged to illustrate issues covered in class.
restrictions: Permission of instructor.

title: Arctic System Science
subject: GEOG
description: The complex Arctic system and its interrelated elements as a coupled system. Topics include: the physical, biological, and social processes that shape the Arctic, including the Arctic atmosphere and ocean, sea ice, permafrost, and terrestrial ecosystems. Unique challenges and opportunities in this fragile and rapidly changing environment, including current research in Arctic science.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: ATOC 215 or ENVR 200 or GEOG 203 or permission of the instructor.

title: Arctic Field Research
subject: GEOG
description: This course is the independent research component of the McGill Arctic Field Study Semester. It has four distinct parts, a) problem identification and background preparation, b) research design and field data collection, c) lab and data analysis, and d) report preparation and presentation. The research design and field data collection will be part of an extended period of fieldwork based in the Canadian Arctic. The Lab and data analysis will begin in the field and finish on campus. Each student will prepare a manuscript style report and make a conference presentation based on their research.
restrictions: Permission of the instructor. Not open to students who have taken or are taking ATOC 473 or EPSC 473.

title: Contested Cities and Urban Activism
subject: GEOG
description: Introduction to key themes in contested cities and urbana ctivism, including struggles for LGBTQ communities; racial, gender, and environmental justice, anti- gentrification movements, and contestations over the use of roads and public spaces. How urban geographers and other academics working in urban fields merge scholarship and activism. A hands-on component that focuses on fieldwork skills and direct engagement with communities.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 217 or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Open to U2 and above students

title: Health and Environment in Africa
subject: GEOG
description: Exploration of key diseases of development, as well as patterns and determinants of health and disease in East Africa. Topics will focus on population and environmental health.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 221, GEOG 303 or permission of instructor
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken GEOG 403. Open to students in the African Field Study Semester (AFSS) only.

title: Urban Field Studies
subject: GEOG
description: Geographical research in urban public and semi-public spaces. Demonstration of techniques of mapping, sampling, measurement, photography, interviewing. Attention to research design.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: One of the following: GEOG 201, GEOG 203, GEOG 210, GEOG 216, GEOG 217, GEOG 272, or permission of instructor

title: Field Studies - Physical Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Field research projects in physical geography. Held locally in Monteregian or Eastern Township regions. The course is organised around field projects designed to formulate and test scientific hypotheses in a physical geography discipline. May Summer session.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Permission of the instructor and 6 credits from the following list of Systematic Physical Geography courses: GEOG 305, GEOG321, GEOG 322, GEOG 372, GEOG 470.

title: Geographical Excursion
subject: GEOG
description: Lecture course on the geography of a region and excursion through the selected country or region including landscape interpretation and field study projects.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 290 and permission of instructor

title: Humans in Tropical Environments
subject: GEOG
description: Focus on understanding of inter-relations between humans and neotropical environments represented in Panama. Study of contemporary rural landscapes, their origins, development and change. Impacts of economic growth and inequality, social organization, and politics on natural resource use and environmental degradation. Site visits and field exercises in peasant/colonist, Amerindian, and plantation communities.
restrictions: Location in Panama. Student must register for a full semester of studies in Panama

title: Advanced Topics in Health Geography
subject: GEOG
description: A critical review of current themes and trends in health geography, with an emphasis on housing as a place-based determinant of health and as a setting for intervention, i.e. how changes in housing conditions can translate into improvements in health and well-being. Seminars focus on critical appraisal of conceptual and methodological approaches in health geography and related disciplines.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 303 or GEOG 403 or permission of instructor
restrictions: Course open to U3 undergraduate students and graduate students in the Department of Geography, or others with permission of the instructor.

title: Advanced Economic Geography
subject: GEOG
description: The objective of this seminar course is to develop an understanding of the geographical dimensions of a variety of new forms of economic and social organization that are emerging across the globe. Key themes focus on innovation, technological and managerial change, evolutionary economic geography, globalization, and changing geographies of inequality.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: GEOG 311 or permission of instructor

title: Global Biogeochemistry
subject: GEOG
description: An examination of the storage, transfers and cycling of major elements and substances, with an emphasis on the global scale and the linkages between the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 305 or GEOG 322 and permission of instructor

title: Advanced Geographic Information Science
subject: GEOG
description: Critically analyse major themes in geographic information science and draw out the practical ramifications for spatial technologies and research. Topics such as spatial interoperability, data quality, scale, visualization, location based services and ontologies are covered.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: (Undergraduate): GEOG 384 or GEOG 414; and permission of the instructor

title: Advanced Social Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Current theories and themes in social geography, such as relations between society and space, social and spatial relations of inequality, difference and diversity, situated and embodied identities, social issues and problems, connections between society and nature, all within a spatial framework.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 331 or equivalent, and permission of instructor.

title: Qualitative Methods
subject: GEOG
description: Critical understandings of methodological approaches and debates involved in qualitative research in geography, including a focus on ethics, positionality, and rigour.

title: Humid Tropical Environments
subject: GEOG
description: Focus on the environmental and human spatial relationships in tropical rain forest and savanna landscapes. Human adaptation to variations within these landscapes through time and space. Biophysical constraints upon "development" in the modern era.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 203 or equivalent and written permission of the instructor

title: Advanced Political Geography
subject: GEOG
description: Questions of space and power in contemporary political geography. Range of topics, including territoriality, the state, the politics of space, critical geopolitics, symbolic landscapes, and GIS and mapping. Emphasizes theoretical issues but includes empirical and/or case studies.
restrictions: Undergraduate students require the permission of the instructor to enroll.

title: Advanced Quantitative Methods in Social Field Research
subject: GEOG
description: How does one collect data to quantitatively assess research questions in human geography or other social sciences, and what methods are available to analyze those data? This course introduces students to advanced statistical techniques commonly confronted in field-based social science studies. The course is divided into four major topics: research design, evaluating impacts of policies or programs, time-series data, and spatial interactions. For the techniques investigated, the course will highlight major technical assumptions, field considerations for data collection, and how each does or does not account for geographic factors that may influence outcomes of interest.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 351 or SOCI 504 or SOCI 505 or ECON 337, or equivalent experience in applied multivariate regression with permission of instructor.

title: Climate Change Vulnerability and Adaptation
subject: GEOG
description: A critical examination of: the theoretical and conceptual evolution of climate change vulnerability and adaptation research; methodological developments from the role of model-driven assessments to the rise of participatory case study research, and the integration of vulnerability research into adaptation planning.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 406 or ECON 347, or equivalent with permission of instructor

title: Contemporary Dilemmas of Development
subject: GEOG
description: Analysis of acute geographic dilemmas of international development. Emphasis on 1) rural systems and the problems of agrobiodiversity, land tenure, conflict, food relief, refugees and migration, the peace process, geopolitics and diplomacy; 2) role of development programs and agendas of the international community, the workings of development On the Ground (TM).
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 310, GEOG 408, or a 400-level course in development
restrictions: Only open to U3 students with permission of instructor.

title: Agriculture, Environment, and Food Security
subject: GEOG
description: This course will consider multiple dimensions of the food security-environment challenge, including the biophysical, economic, nutritional, socio-political, and policy/institutional. It will use a global perspective, drawing upon both global-scale research as well as case studies from different regions of the world to understand the geography of agricultural production, its environmental footprint, and of malnutrition.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): ENVR 201, and NUTR 341 or any 300 or 400-level course in agricultural science, ecology, environment, economics, geography, or nutrition, or with permission of instructor.
restrictions: Restricted to U2 and U3 students.

title: Advanced Environmental Hydrology
subject: GEOG
description:
Traditional and emerging theories of dominant runoff generation processes. Streamflow generation. Surface and near-surface solute and contaminant transport. Concentration-discharge relationships. Geochemical mixing models. Dyes and biological tracers of water.
Isotope ecohydrology. Water source and water age estimation approaches. Development, execution, and evaluation of process-based watershed models. Case
studies from forested, agricultural and periurban watersheds.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: BREE 217, BREE 509, EPSC 549 or GEOG 322, or permission of the instructor.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking EPSC 522.

title: Asian Cities in the 21st Century
subject: GEOG
description: This course examines current themes relating to mass urbanization in Asia in a range of contexts and the forces that shape the built environment of Asian cities. Various approaches to understanding Asian cities and current theoretical debates will be investigated, including recent critiques of western-centric theorizations of urban change in the region. The course examines a variety of themes through which students will gain familiarity with some of the major strands relating to urban change in Asia: national identity, neoliberalism, social exclusions, migration, religion, ethnicity and sustainability.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 325, or 9 credits of Geography courses in Urban Geography, or permission of the instructor.

title: Global Land and Water Resources
subject: GEOG
description: Linkage of physical processes (hydrology and ecosystems) with issues of societal and socio-economic relevance (land, food, and water use appropriation for human well-being). Application of a holistic perspective on land, food and water issues in an international setting, highlighting linkages, feedbacks and trade-offs in an Earth system context.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): GEOG 203 or ESYS 200 or ENVR 200 or equivalent; GEOG 322 or BREE 217 or equivalent; or permission of instructor.

title: Remote Sensing and Interpretation
subject: GEOG
description: Basic photogrammetry and interpretation procedures for aircraft and space craft photography and imagery.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 308 and written permission of instructor

title: Geocryology
subject: GEOG
description: Study of the unique geomorphic aspects of periglacial and permafrost environments. The focus will be on processes in cold climates, the impact of human activity on permafrost landscapes and potential impacts of climatic change.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GEOG 272 and any 300-level geomorphology course approved by instructor

subject: GEOG
description: A broad overview of ecological restoration. Considers causes of environmental degradation, why and what we restore, how restoration goals are set, and standards in restoration practice, as well as critiques and philosophies of ecological restoration, such as "ecocultural" restoration.

Techniques for studying plant communities are emphasized and applied to 3 different types of wetlands through field and laboratory work.

subject: GERM
description: The seminar examines images and narratives of the foreign, alien, and uncanny Other in major works of German literature, film, music, and art from Romanticism to the present. Works discussed include Wagner's Lohengrin, expressionist art, and texts by authors such as ETA Hoffmann, Kleist, Freud, Nietzsche, Kafka, and Thomas Mann.

title: German Language - Intensive Advanced
subject: GERM
description: This course aims at developing post-intermediate proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills, with emphasis on oral and written expression. Special attention is given to word formation and to the proper choice of grammatical structures, vocabulary, and phraseology.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: GERM 300 or GERM 307D1/D2, or equivalent, or permission of Department.

title: Topics: German Language and Culture
subject: GERM
description:
This course aims to both improve students’ speaking and writing skills at the intermediate and advanced levels and to deepen their understanding of German culture through contemporary short texts and films. Topics include migration and national identity, memory and history, gender roles, and intergenerational conflicts. Students develop their transcultural competencies through critical
engagement with the course materials. Selected grammatical topics will be reviewed.

title: Germany after Reunification
subject: GERM
description: The events which led to the fall of the Berlin Wall, the reunification of Germany in 1990 and the changing cultural, social, political and economic landscape of the 'New Germany'. Highlighting issues of cultural and social politics, texts discussed include historical, literary and film material.

title: Topics in Eighteenth-Century German Literature and Culture

title: Science and Literature
subject: GERM
description: This course examines the complex exchanges between science and literature across German literature and culture.

title: German Language, Media and Culture
subject: GERM
description: Introduction to German culture through literary and non-literary texts, film, multimedia, commercials, painting and photography. By learning how to read these cultural productions, students will refine their communication skills, expand reading strategies, build vocabulary, and review selective grammatical structures.

title: Literature and Revolution
subject: GERM
description: Seminar on the relationship between literature and political, social and aesthetic change.

title: Romanticism

title: Realism

description: What are the different ways social life has been represented in German literature and culture?

subject: GERM

title: Berlin

description: Interdisciplinary study of the quintessential modern centers within Germanic speaking Europe.

title: German Literature - 19th Century 3
subject: GERM
description: This course offers an introduction to the literary movements of Biedermeier, Junges Deutschland, Vormärz, Poetic Realism, and Naturalism in connection with the political and social developments in 19th century Germany. Tests by major authors such as Buchner, Heine and Fontane will be discussed.

title: Nietzsche and Wagner
subject: GERM
description: This course examines the relationship between the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche and the composer Richard Wagner. It explores their intellectual kinship, their view of art, music, and philosophy in the context of Nietzsche's critique of modernity and decadence and analyzes the Third Reich's and Hollywood's appropriation of Nietzsche and Wagner.

title: German Culture in European Context
subject: GERM
description: A comparative examination of selected moments in German literary, artistic and cultural history in relation to broader European movements; focus on influences, exchanges and dialogues across national boundaries.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: A culture or literature course at the 200 or 300 level

title: Franz Kafka
subject: GERM
description: This course will look at the works on Franz Kafka, a "classic" modernist author, in three characteristic genres: the story, the novel, and the short prose piece. A selection of Kafka's letters and diary entries as well as critical approaches to his work will also be studied.

title: German Drama
subject: GERM
description: This course will survey the theatrical tradition within German.

title: Weimar Literature and Culture
subject: GERM
description: The course deals with the culture, literature and society of the Weimar Republic and the period of the Third Reich and the Holocaust. Writers studied will include: Brecht, Seghers, Fleisser, Kästner, Tucholsky, Benn, Kolmar, and Lasker-Schüler.

title: 20th Century Literature Topics
subject: GERM

title: German Postwar Literature
subject: GERM
description: The course deals with the literature and culture of the Federal Republic of Germany, the former German Democratic Republic and unified Germany since 1945. It treats major authors and trends. Topics addressed include issues of nationalism and gender, multiculturalism, and other concerns of contemporary German society.

title: Gender and Society in German Literature and Culture
subject: GERM
description: In connection with notions of identity, nationhood, political change, and cultural difference, this course investigates concepts and issues of gender in contemporary German Society. The readings include critical essays and literary texts by writers, scholars, philosophers, journalists, politicians, and political activists.

title: Weimar German Cinema
subject: GERM
description: Weimar Cinema brought to the screen a world populated by monsters, lunatics, workers, vamps, strangers, and doubles. These figures embodied the tensions and fears of the Weimar period (1919-1933) in a manner that continues to attract audiences today. This course explores the cultural and political history of the Weimar period through Weimar cinema. It aims to introduce the student to the fundamentals of film analysis, especially formal analysis and textual analysis.

title: Foundations in Population and Global Health
subject: GPHL
description: Exploration of global policies, politics, industry and institutions and their neo-colonial underpinnings, and their influence on current global health theory, research and practice, with a special focus on the health of Indigenous peoples in Canada and other racialized groups. The environmental and social determinants of health and health inequities, with attention to women and children’s health, communicable and non-communicable disease, and the complexities of disasters and humanitarian crises. Global health governance,systems, and innovations and social entrepreneurship in health.

title: Population and Global Health Ethics
subject: GPHL
description:
An introduction to the concepts of ethics and equity, in a broad range of applications, including power, privilege and positionality. Exploration of
foundations of ethics as they apply to population and global health practice. Concepts of human rights, anti-racism, ethics and equity, informed by an
understanding of the legacy of colonization, as they pertain to a wide array of global health issues.

title: Data Literacy
subject: GPHL
description: Introduction to foundational concepts in statistical thinking, data science and epidemiology including how to connect data to underlying phenomena and dealing with illustrating and interpreting data.
restrictions: Open to students in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Introduction to Research Methods
subject: GPHL
description: Introduction to quantitative, qualitative and participatory research approaches to population and global health problem solving, with a focus on critical skills in assessing research quality and relevance. Concepts include: the art of formulating a research question, and its implications for research design and implementation.
restrictions: Open to students in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Knowledge Translation
subject: GPHL
description: Key knowledge translation concepts, principles and practice as they apply to the formulation of policies and programs serving disadvantaged populations in resource-constrained settings. Interdisciplinary sharing and critical appraisal and application of existing knowledge to the development of global and public health policies, program content and its delivery.
restrictions: Open to students enrolled in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Community Engaged Learning
subject: GPHL
description: Introduction to community engaged learning with a focus on the broader determinants of health. Exploration of the social, environmental and structural determinants of health and health inequities in the local community context. Exposure to the complexities of meaningful, ethical and productive community partnership, teamwork skills and workplace professionalism.
restrictions: Open to students in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Critical Perspectives in Global Health
subject: GPHL
description: Examination of critical issues in global health animated by invited research, policy and practice experts from low- and middle-income countries, including the decolonization of global health and power imbalances in global health governance, funding, research, teaching. Competencies in critical thinking, problem-solving interdisciplinarity and managing complexity will be emphasized. The unfinished agendas of tuberculosis, malaria, HIV, reproductive, child and adolescent health, and current global challenges, including pandemics, humanitarian crises and refugee health, environmental health and climate change, chronic disease, mental health, access to technologies, and global health governance, advocacy, and delivery.
restrictions: Open to students in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Experiential Learning
subject: GPHL
description: A full-semester capstone practicum undertaken in the context of a community organization, mentored research activity or an internship with an international or local public health agency, focusing on a relevant global health-related issue, and skills in professional conduct, team work, effective communication and knowledge translation.
restrictions: Open to students in a Population and Global Health undergraduate program.

title: Critical Perspectives in Global Health

description: Global health issues, including global burden of diseases, determinants of health, transition in health and drivers of such transition, challenges in healthcare delivery in resource-limited settings, and the variety of agencies and actors engaged in addressing global health challenges.

title: Beyond the Human Genome
subject: HGEN
description: A review of recent advances in human genomics and current state of the art technologies of DNA sequence and whole genomics analyses, as well as future directions in the post-genomic era.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: BIOL 370 or by permission of the instructor.

title: Advances in Human Genetics 1
subject: HGEN
description: This course will deal with recent progress in human genetics, and its applications to health care, by identifying different fields including different disciplines (e.g. cancer genetics, neurogenetics), different conceptual approaches, or different methodologic approaches.

title: Methods and Concepts in Epigenetic Regulation Studies
subject: HGEN
description: Advanced concepts in epigenetics and chromatin regulation, experimental methods used in epigenetics research, and computational methods for analysis of epigenomics data.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken or are taking PHAR 565.

title: Research Internship
subject: HGEN
description: Research Internship on the ethico-legal and policy issues in human genetics in both the research and the clinical settings.

title: Stem Cell Biology
subject: HGEN
description: Introduction to the field of stem cell research. Definition of stem cells. Pluripotent stem cells and reprogramming. Adult stem cells, niche and asymmetric division. Clinical applications of stem cells. Cancer stem cells. Ethical issues surrounding stem cell research and clinical treatment.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: HGEN692 or equivalent Minimum grade attained by student must be: B+

title: Lab Course in Genomics
subject: HGEN
description: Introduction to Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) Based Genomics in the form of seminars and laboratory work. Lectures in state of the art sequencing technologies and their applications. Laboratory work in the preparation of high quality libraries for analyzing DNA and large/small RNAs. Hands on experience in setting up next Generation Sequencing using specialized equipment. Tutorials in use of Bio-informatics Analysis tools in experimental design, quality control, and in depth analysis of data. Practicum in using computational tools for personalized data analyses. Technology paper presentation, as well as production of a report on course data generation and analysis.

title: Statistical Concepts in Genetic and Genomic Analysis
subject: HGEN
description: This course will introduce key statistical concepts that motivate and underlie the many statistical analysis methods currently used in analysis of genetic and genomic data. Emphasis will be placed on understanding how these concepts can influence study designs and analysis choices, and when substantial unanticipated biases can occur. Concepts include an understanding of variability and error, bias and its sources, independence, how distributions of variables impact analysis, outliers, covariates, missing data, the goals of data cleaning, multiple testing, and some consideration of clustering and prediction models.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite(s): A course introducing basic statistics or equivalent knowledge. Registration is by permission of the course coordinator.

title: Neurogenetics
subject: HGEN
description:
Focus on advanced methods in genetics and their applications to understand the genetics of the brain in health and disease. Topics include high throughput
sequencing, genome-wide association studies, disease models, organoids, RNA sequencing, single-cell sequencing and more to better understand the brain.
restrictions: Open to all graduate students enrolled in Human Genetics and students in other graduate programs, with permission from the course coordinator.

title: Cancer Genetics: Precision Oncology
subject: HGEN
description: The past, present, and future of cancer research and treatment with an emphasis on precision medicine driven by significant advances in genomics. Precision medicine uses genomics, RNA and protein abundance, as well as key metabolic and physiological markers to best design and implement treatment.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Approval of the course instructor.

title: Contemporary Brazilian Literature and Film
subject: HISP
description: This course introduces students to Brazilian literature and film from the early 20th century to the present day. Students will examine literary works and films from a historical perspective, studying the social, political and regional processes in which they are embedded. From the barren Northeast, to an analysis of gender and race, to urban violence and its manifestations to the contemporary cityscape, this course covers a range of visual and textual material. Students will engage works from major Brazilian authors and filmmakers in conjunction with theoretical texts to better understand some of the main developments in contemporary cultural production.

subject: HISP
description: The Romantic, Realist and Naturalist novel in Spain, with special emphasis on the development of the Spanish novel in relation to contemporary trends in other European countries.
restrictions: Not open to students who have taken HISP 325

prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Successful completion of any Survey of Literature (HISP 241, HISP 242, HISP 243, HISP 244) or permission of the instructor. Note: Course taught in Spanish.

title: Contemporary Hispanic Cultural Studies
subject: HISP
description: This course examines contemporary Hispanic Cultural Studies looking at both cultural artifacts and diverse theoretical and methodological approaches. In doing so, it will introduce students to the frameworks necessary for approaching contemporary culture in the Hispanic World. The course will be mindful of issues including ideology, class, race, ethnicity and sexuality. Students will come into contact with the major cultural theorists in the Hispanic World and those issues pertinent to the study of culture.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Successful completion of one of the Survey of Literature courses (HISP 241, HISP 242, HISP 243, HISP 244), or permission of the instructor

Contemporary Spanish
 Literature and Culture

prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Successful completion of one of the Survey of Literature courses (HISP 241, HISP 242, HISP 243, HISP 244), or permission of the instructor.

subject: HISP

prerequisitesText: Prerequisite: Successful completion of any Survey of Literature (HISP 241, HISP 242, HISP 243, HISP 244) or permission of the instructor. Note: Course taught in Spanish.

subject: HISP
description: This course will examine digital cultural production in Latin America from 1990 to the present day. This course introduces students to theoretical frameworks necessary for approaching new media and web-based cultural artifacts, both literary and visual. Students will come into contact with the major writers, artists and web-based cultural producers in Latin America and issues pertinent to the study of the Web in the region.
prerequisitesText: Prerequisites: Successful completion of one of the Survey of Literature courses (HISP 241, HISP 242, HISP 243, HISP 244), or permission of the instructor.

subject: HISP

title: FYS: Nation Building and Nationalism
subject: HIST
description: An introduction to some of the major theories of nationalism; an exploration of the many varieties of nationalism and forms of nation-building; a particular focus on the historical background to case studies of current interest.
restrictions: Open only to newly admitted students in U0 or U1, who may take only one FYS. Students who register for more than one will be obliged to withdraw from all but one of them.
